title: Backlit photography
summary: Shoot into the light for rim glow, silhouettes and sun stars.

blocks.text: With the light **behind** the subject you get glowing edges (rim light), silhouettes, glowing fur and hair, and sun stars. The challenge is exposure: the camera sees a bright sky and darkens everything.

items: A **low sun**: golden hour after sunrise or before sunset.
Clear or partly cloudy skies. Heavy cloud kills the effect.
A **dark, clean background** behind the subject so the rim light shows.
Fuzzy or see-through subjects: fur, hair, leaves, petals, breath on a cold morning.
Dust, mist or pollen in the air for glowing layers.
Use **M** mode, or Av with exposure compensation.
Subject detail: start at **+1 EV**. Dark background: start at **−1 EV**.
**Evaluative** metering keeps the sky; **spot** on the subject exposes it but whites out the sky.
Shoot **RAW** and bracket ±1 stop when unsure.
Turn on highlight alerts (blinkies) and watch the rim.

blocks.title: Quick tips
items: Put the sun 15–20° to the side of the subject, still behind it, for the best rim light.
Get low to clean up the background.
Silhouettes work when the shape alone tells you what it is.
It's fine to leave the subject a little dark. Shape matters more than detail.
Near water, reflections double the light.
Before sunrise the light is softer and easier to expose.

blocks.text: Close down to f/9–f/18 and hide about half the sun behind an edge. Move a few centimetres until the star is strongest.

The camera's meter tries to make a bright sky mid-grey, so the subject goes dark. That's fine for a silhouette. For detail you're balancing on a tightrope: a little brighter and the sky blows out, a little darker and the subject goes black.

items: Evaluative metering is the forgiving choice: it underexposes the subject, but dark areas recover better in editing than blown-out whites.
Spot metering on a mid-tone of the subject exposes it properly but usually leaves the sky white (a high-key look, which can be the goal).
A thin rim that's slightly overexposed is fine.
Fill flash or a reflector adds light to the front of the subject. Use less than you think.
Lower highlights, lift shadows. Keep it natural.
Add contrast or clarity to the subject only (a subject mask).
Negative clarity gives a soft, dreamy look.
Warm the white balance for sunsets; try cool shadows against a warm sun.
A vignette or graduated filter steers the eye and balances the sky.
Exposures blended from a bracket (HDR) hold both sun and shadows.
